blocks.text: “Thank your ladyship.” Mr. Guppy does so. “Now, your ladyship.” Mr. Guppy looks at a little piece of paper. On it he has written short notes of the points he wants to make. But every time he looks at it, it seems to leave him completely confused. “I—oh yes!—I put myself completely in your ladyship's hands. Your ladyship might complain to Kenge and Carboy, or to Mr. Tulkinghorn, about this visit. If you did, I would be in a very unpleasant position. I admit that openly. So I depend on your ladyship's honour.”
My Lady makes a scornful movement with the hand that holds the screen. In this way she tells him that he is not worth any complaint from her.

“Thank your ladyship,” says Mr. Guppy, “that is quite satisfactory. Now—I—dash it!—The fact is, I wrote down one or two headings here. They give the order of the points I wanted to speak about. But they are written in a short form, and I can't quite make out what they mean. If your ladyship will excuse me, I will take the paper to the window for half a moment. I—”

Mr. Guppy goes to the window and bumps into a pair of love-birds. In his confusion he says to them, “I beg your pardon, I am sure.” This does not help him read his notes any better. He grows warm and red and murmurs to himself. He holds the piece of paper now close to his eyes, now a long way off. “C. S. What's C. S. for? Oh! ‘E. S!’ Oh, I know! Yes, of course!” And he comes back with the mystery solved.
“I do not know,” says Mr. Guppy, standing halfway between my Lady and his chair, “whether your ladyship ever happened to hear of, or to see, a young lady called Miss Esther Summerson.”
My Lady looks straight at him. “I saw a young lady of that name not long ago. This past autumn.”
“Now, did your ladyship notice that she looked like anybody?” asks Mr. Guppy. He crosses his arms, holds his head on one side, and scratches the corner of his mouth with his notes.
From this moment, My Lady does not take her eyes off him.
“I think,” says Mr. Guppy, “that your ladyship can hardly remember Miss Summerson's face?”
“I remember the young lady very well. What has this to do with me?”

“Your ladyship, I assure you of this. Miss Summerson's image is printed on my 'art—I mention that in confidence. Now, I once went on a short trip to the county of Lincolnshire with a friend. While I was there, I had the honour of going round your ladyship's great house, Chesney Wold. There I saw such a likeness between Miss Esther Summerson and your ladyship's own portrait that it completely knocked me over. In fact, at that moment I did not even know what it was that had knocked me over. And now I have the honour of seeing your ladyship close up. (Since then, I have often taken the liberty of looking at your ladyship in your carriage in the park. I dare say you were not aware of me. But I never saw your ladyship so near.) Now that I see you, the likeness is really more surprising than I thought.”

Young man called Guppy! There were times, long ago, when ladies lived in strong castles and had servants within call who would do anything, however wicked. In those times, your poor life would not have been worth a minute's purchase, with those beautiful eyes looking at you as they look at you now.
My Lady slowly uses her little hand-screen as a fan. She asks him again: what does he suppose his interest in likenesses has to do with her?

“Your ladyship,” replies Mr. Guppy, looking at his paper again, “I am coming to that. Dash these notes. Oh! ‘Mrs. Chadband.’ Yes.” Mr. Guppy pulls his chair a little forward and sits down again. My Lady leans back calmly in her chair. But perhaps she sits with a little less of her usual graceful ease. Her steady gaze never wavers. “A—stop a minute, though!” Mr. Guppy looks at his notes again. “E. S. twice? Oh yes! Yes, I see my way now, right on.”
